Fifteen decades ago, Francis Galton first came up with the term “nature versus nurture”, and this debate over the factors shaping human identity has long been a central topic in human sciences.

Through this new perspective, nature and nurture are hardly separable at all – genes and the environment do not act independently, but instead interact closely and even shape one another in tangible ways.

Through this new perspective, nature and nurture are hardly separable at all – genes and the environment do not act independently, but instead interact closely and even shape one another in tangible ways.
Genes do not shape our identities merely on their own within our bodies; instead, they function partly by molding the environments we choose or create.
Initial research suggests that your partner’s genes influence your likelihood of depression almost a third as much as your own genes do.

A few students with a genetic trend for smoking in a high school seemed to cause smoking rates to skyrocket across the entire grade – even among students who have no direct contact with these students – like a gene-driven wildfire spreading through social networks.
Nature and nurture both shape each other, with nature influencing the way we experience nurture and nurture influencing the way our nature expresses itself.
